attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own article, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Dropping 'becoming increasingly apparent' removes the framing but not the claim itself. That phrase says the evidence is mounting; it is not a probability hedge. This is a present-tense observation about profitability.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: operating profit at the major standalone developers (OpenAI, Anthropic) in H1 2025, the latest period reported before the post. Leaving out parent-company profits fits the context. An unknown accounting basis does not block scoring, because the losses are large under every basis shown.

evidence.note: Secondary report, citing The Information, of a $7.8B OpenAI operating loss in H1 2025. It is an estimate, but it covers the target period and metric. Available before the evaluation date.
Anthropic's S-1 shows GAAP operating losses of $935M in Q1 2025 and $1.2B in Q2 2025, i.e. after full operating costs. Filed 2026-10-26, before the evaluation date.

reviews.rationale: Both leading standalone LLM developers had large operating losses after full operating costs in H1 2025: OpenAI about $7.8B (reported) and Anthropic about $2.1B (filed). Together they give enough coverage for the ordinary reading of the generalisation, and the packet holds no counterevidence. The unknown accounting basis does not change the sign of the result.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own article.

semantics.note: The revision keeps 'that I can see', 'seems' and the scope of his roughly two-year dataset. It is an observation about Anthropic's cost-cutting and burn, limited to the data he has seen.

contract.note: Reading 'burn' as net cash consumption is ordinary. But the speaker's data is AWS bills, so 'burn' may loosely mean cloud spending, and cash-flow timing (prepayments) could swing the result. This interpretation was not supplied by the speaker.

evidence.note: The S-1 cash flows show operating cash use rose in 2024 and fell in 2025, mostly because of prepaid hosting timing rather than cost reductions. These are annual and half-year figures, not a matched monthly series.
The speaker's own reported AWS series shows a few month-to-month dips in 2024. It is not independently verified and is not total net burn.

reviews.rationale: No monthly net cash-burn series for Jan 2024 to Sep 2025 is in the packet. Average monthly operating cash use was lower in H1 2025 than in 2024, but the filing attributes this to using up prepaid hosting, not to cost-cutting. The AWS dips are unverified and are not total burn. The evidence neither confirms nor refutes the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The Cursor premise is his own tentative account.

semantics.note: 'I believe this is what awaits any product' is a firm expectation, so it is a forecast. The drafter's modality 'likely' understates its firmness, though the proposition keeps 'I believe'. The 'may have' applies only to the Cursor analogy.

contract.note: The 30-day coincidence window and the definition of a qualifying price increase were added by the evaluator. 'Any product' with no deadline makes the claim hard to settle. The early-resolution rule is reasonable.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own announcement of Opus 4.5 and Claude Code updates. It lowers list prices and shows no increase imposed on a competing customer, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: This is an open-ended forecast with no deadline, and no dated event meets the early-resolution rule. The packet has no paired records of a price increase coinciding with a competing launch, and no definitive counterexample. It cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own reporting and causal account in his own article.

semantics.note: Combines factual billing figures with a causal chain (Priority Tiers, then a cash crunch, made worse by the AWS bills). 'Rent-seeking' and 'Subprime AI Crisis' are evaluative labels.

contract.note: Defining a cash crunch as liquidity pressure is the ordinary meaning. The requirements for the billing figures and the causal chain are fair to his words.

evidence.note: Cursor's own disclosure attributes its repricing to higher token use per request. This is a competing or additional cause; it does not verify the bills or disprove the claim.
Cursor's own disclosure of a $900M raise on June 6, 2025 cuts against a liquidity shortage but does not disclose cash obligations, so it does not disprove the claim.

reviews.rationale: No independent record confirms the $6.2M and $12.6M AWS figures or a Cursor cash crunch, and nothing ties Priority Service Tiers causally to Cursor's finances. The Series C raise and the token-cost explanation cast doubt on the account but do not disprove it.
